name: LiteLLM RCE
tile_line: In CISA KEV, due 2 Dec. Public PoC, needs admin key.
tldr: A sandbox escape in the LiteLLM proxy runs any command, as root in the default Docker image. It needs an admin key, but attackers are guessing default ones. Public exploit, on CISA's exploited list. Upgrade to the newest on your line.
summary: LiteLLM's proxy has an endpoint for testing custom guardrail code, and its home-made sandbox can be escaped to run any command, as root in the default Docker image. It needs a proxy-admin key, but attackers have been guessing default keys, and two other bugs let ordinary users become admin on older versions.

affected.label: LiteLLM 1.81.8 – 1.83.10
affected.text: GitHub's advisory lists >= 1.81.8, < 1.83.10 as affected, but its text says the fix is in 1.83.11, so count 1.83.10 as affected to be safe. Only the proxy server is at risk, not plain use of the Python SDK. In Docker, image tags don't reliably match versions (`main-latest` tells you nothing), so check the pip version inside the container.

affected.label: Management API is reachable
affected.text: The attacker can reach the proxy's management API, including `POST /guardrails/test_custom_code`. Keep it off untrusted networks.

affected.label: Attacker has an admin key
affected.text: The default config requires a proxy-admin credential (the master key). These also count: a weak key like `sk-1234`; no master key at all (callers are treated as admin); any user account below 1.83.14 (CVE-2026-47101/47102) or on 1.91.0 up to the CVE-2026-114612 fix; Enterprise-licensed proxies below 1.106.5, which can leak the master key to anyone; and proxies below 1.106.9 with an Azure model but no Azure API key set, where any logged-in user can read the master key.

do.label: Upgrade to the newest on your line
do.text: 1.83.11 fixed this sandbox escape, but later releases had their own admin-takeover bugs. Use at least 1.106.9, 1.108.6 or 1.109.1 (listed below). These also cover the older LiteLLM KEV entries CVE-2026-42208 and CVE-2026-42271 (fixed 1.83.7) and CVE-2026-59822 (fixed 1.84.0).

do.label: Until then: block the endpoint
do.text: Block `POST /guardrails/test_custom_code` at your reverse proxy or API gateway. Keep the admin port off the internet. If you use Azure models, also block the fields `tenant_id`, `client_id`, `client_secret`, `azure_username`, `azure_password` and `azure_scope` in request bodies.

do.label: Rotate a weak or old master key
do.text: Attackers sprayed default-style keys at this endpoint. If yours is guessable or was exposed, replace it. The escape exposes provider and cloud keys stored in the proxy, so rotate those too.

do.label: Run the container as non-root
do.text: The default image runs as root, so a sandbox escape gets root. LiteLLM also ships a non-root image.

slack: LiteLLM CVE-2026-40217: a sandbox escape in the proxy's /guardrails/test_custom_code endpoint lets anyone with an admin key run commands, as root in the default Docker image. Public PoC, attempts seen, added to CISA KEV on 18 Nov (due 2 Dec). Affected: 1.81.8 through 1.83.10. Upgrade to at least 1.106.9, 1.108.6 or 1.109.1, since later releases had their own admin-takeover bugs. Until then, block that endpoint and rotate any weak master key. Check with `pip show litellm`.
